strumenti/rubin/tipo: 8.4-metre telescope with the largest camera in the world
strumenti/rubin/cosa: A wide-field telescope that photographs the whole sky visible from Chile every three or four nights, for ten years, turning it into a colour "film". Its camera has 3,200 megapixels, hundreds of times more than a phone.
strumenti/rubin/dove: On Cerro Pachón, at about 2,700 metres, in the Andes of Chile.
strumenti/rubin/quando: First images on 23 June 2025. The great survey of the sky, called the LSST, lasts ten years.
strumenti/rubin/scoperte: In its first 10 hours of testing it found more than 2,000 asteroids never seen before. It will track down millions of asteroids and supernovae and help map dark matter.
strumenti/rubin/origine: Named after Vera Rubin (1928–2016), the American astronomer who, by measuring how galaxies rotate, found some of the strongest evidence that dark matter exists. It is the first US national observatory named after a woman.
strumenti/rubin/curiosita: Every night it produces about 20 terabytes of data, and within minutes it sends out an automatic alert for every object that changes in the sky.
strumenti/elt/cosa: It will be the largest optical telescope in the world: a 39-metre mirror made up of 798 hexagonal segments. It will collect more light than all of today's large telescopes put together. It is being built by ESO.
strumenti/elt/dove: On Cerro Armazones, at 3,046 metres, in the Atacama Desert in Chile, 20 km from the VLT.
strumenti/elt/quando: Work began in 2014. According to ESO, the first test observations are planned for 2029 and the first scientific observations for December 2030.
strumenti/elt/scoperte: None yet: it will look for the atmospheres of Earth-like planets around other stars and for the first galaxies in the universe.
strumenti/elt/origine: Extremely Large Telescope: after the Very Large Telescope, astronomers just kept going up the scale of adjectives. An earlier project, never built, was called OWL, "Overwhelmingly Large".
strumenti/elt/curiosita: Italy plays a leading role: the dome and the structure are being built by a consortium that includes Italian companies, and INAF is leading the construction of MORFEO, the instrument that will correct the shimmering of the air.
strumenti/virgo/nome: Virgo and LIGO, the gravitational-wave detectors
strumenti/virgo/cosa: They are not telescopes: they are two long L-shaped tubes, in a vacuum, with laser beams running along them. When a gravitational wave passes, a tiny ripple in space predicted by Einstein, the arms stretch and shrink by less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton.
strumenti/virgo/dove: Virgo is at Cascina, near Pisa, with 3 km arms: it is Italian-French (INFN and CNRS) with other European countries. The two LIGO detectors are in the United States, at Hanford and Livingston, with 4 km arms.
strumenti/virgo/quando: The first gravitational wave was picked up by LIGO on 14 September 2015. Virgo joined the observations in 2017.
strumenti/virgo/scoperte: The first merger of two black holes, 1.3 billion light years away (Nobel Prize 2017). On 17 August 2017, with Virgo, the collision of two neutron stars, which was then also seen by telescopes: it revealed that collisions like this make gold and platinum.
strumenti/virgo/origine: Virgo takes its name from the Virgo Cluster of galaxies. LIGO stands for Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory.
strumenti/virgo/curiosita: Italy has put forward Sardinia (the Sos Enattos mine, near Lula) as the home for the Einstein Telescope, the future European detector, underground and with 10 km arms.
strumenti/hubble/luce: Visible light, ultraviolet and near infrared
strumenti/hubble/cosa: A telescope with a 2.4-metre mirror, the size of a bus, that orbits the Earth above the atmosphere: up there the stars don't twinkle and the image is pin-sharp. It belongs to NASA, with ESA as a partner.
strumenti/hubble/dove: In orbit around the Earth at a height of about 530 km; it goes round once every 95 minutes.
strumenti/hubble/quando: Launched on 24 April 1990 aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery. Astronauts have repaired and upgraded it five times, most recently in 2009.
strumenti/hubble/scoperte: It measured the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years) and helped discover that its expansion is speeding up (Nobel Prize 2011). With the Hubble Deep Field (1995) it revealed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky that looked empty. It photographed comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashing into Jupiter (1994) and the "Pillars of Creation".
strumenti/hubble/origine: Named after Edwin Hubble, who in the 1920s showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.
strumenti/hubble/curiosita: Just after launch its view was blurred: the mirror was off by about 2 thousandths of a millimetre, a fiftieth of the thickness of a hair. In 1993 astronauts fitted it with corrective "glasses".
strumenti/webb/cosa: The largest telescope ever sent into space: a 6.5-metre mirror made up of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments. It sees in the infrared, the light of heat, and to do so it has to stay colder than 230 degrees below zero, shaded by a sunshield the size of a tennis court. It belongs to NASA, ESA and the Canadian Space Agency.
strumenti/webb/dove: 1.5 million km from the Earth, on the side away from the Sun, at a balance point called L2 (the second Lagrange point).
strumenti/webb/quando: Launched on 25 December 2021 from Kourou, in French Guiana, on a European Ariane 5 rocket. First images in July 2022.
strumenti/webb/scoperte: It has seen galaxies that formed about 300 million years after the Big Bang, many more than expected. In 2022 it found carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of a planet around another star (WASP-39b). It is also studying the atmospheres of the TRAPPIST-1 planets.
strumenti/webb/origine: Named after James E. Webb, who led NASA from 1961 to 1968, the years when the Apollo programme was being prepared.
strumenti/webb/curiosita: The Ariane 5 rocket put it on course so precisely that it saved fuel: it will be able to work for more than twenty years.
strumenti/chandra/cosa: A telescope that sees X-rays, the light given off by gas heated to millions of degrees: around black holes, in supernova remnants, in clusters of galaxies. The atmosphere blocks X-rays, so they can only be seen from space.
strumenti/chandra/dove: On a very elongated orbit around the Earth, which takes it out to more than a third of the distance to the Moon.
strumenti/chandra/quando: Launched on 23 July 1999 aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia, on the first Shuttle mission commanded by a woman, Eileen Collins.
strumenti/chandra/scoperte: In 2006 the Bullet Cluster, two clusters of galaxies that have collided, provided direct evidence of dark matter. It photographed the neutron star at the centre of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A.
strumenti/chandra/origine: Named after the Indian astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, Nobel Prize 1983, who studied how stars die. "Chandra" means Moon, or shining, in Sanskrit. The name was chosen through a competition won by a student and a teacher.
strumenti/chandra/curiosita: The telescope was proposed in 1976 by the Italian Riccardo Giacconi, the father of X-ray astronomy, Nobel Prize 2002.
strumenti/spitzer/cosa: An infrared telescope with an 85 cm mirror, cooled almost to absolute zero. It could see through the clouds of dust where stars are born.
strumenti/spitzer/dove: On an orbit around the Sun, trailing behind the Earth and slowly drifting away from it.
strumenti/spitzer/scoperte: In 2017 it helped discover the seven rocky planets of the star TRAPPIST-1. In 2009 it found a gigantic, thin, invisible ring around Saturn, made by the moon Phoebe. It was one of the first telescopes to measure the light of a planet around another star.
strumenti/spitzer/origine: Named after Lyman Spitzer, the astronomer who as early as 1946 proposed putting telescopes in space, above the atmosphere.
strumenti/spitzer/curiosita: Its coolant ran out in 2009, but Spitzer kept working for more than ten years with the instruments that still worked "warm".
strumenti/kepler/cosa: A telescope that stared at the same patch of sky, between Cygnus and Lyra, measuring the light of 150,000 stars. When a planet passes in front of its star, the light dips very slightly: this is the transit method.
strumenti/kepler/dove: On an orbit around the Sun, trailing behind the Earth.
strumenti/kepler/quando: Launched on 7 March 2009, switched off on 30 October 2018 when it ran out of fuel.
strumenti/kepler/scoperte: More than 2,600 confirmed planets: it showed that there are more planets than stars. Kepler-186f (2014) was the first Earth-sized planet found in the zone where liquid water could exist. Kepler-16b orbits two suns, like the planet Tatooine in Star Wars.
strumenti/kepler/origine: Named after Johannes Kepler, who in the early 17th century discovered the laws of planetary motion.
strumenti/kepler/curiosita: In 2013 two of the wheels that kept it pointed broke down. The engineers came up with a trick: using the pressure of sunlight as a third wheel. That was how the K2 mission was born, which lasted another five years.
strumenti/tess/cosa: Kepler's successor. With four cameras it observes almost the whole sky, one strip at a time for 27 days, looking for planets passing in front of nearby, bright stars, which are easier to study afterwards with other telescopes.
strumenti/tess/dove: On a very elongated orbit around the Earth, which it completes in 13.7 days, "in time" with the Moon.
strumenti/tess/scoperte: Hundreds of confirmed planets and thousands of candidates. In 2020 it found TOI-700 d, an Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone of its star, about 100 light years away.
strumenti/tess/origine: TESS stands for Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite.
strumenti/tess/curiosita: Its orbit, in resonance with the Moon, is so stable that it could stay there for decades without using any fuel.
strumenti/gaia/nome: Gaia, the map of the Milky Way
strumenti/gaia/cosa: An ESA satellite that measured the position, distance, motion and colour of almost two billion stars, building the most accurate three-dimensional map of our galaxy.
strumenti/gaia/dove: At the L2 point, 1.5 million km from the Earth, like the James Webb.
strumenti/gaia/quando: Launched on 19 December 2013; it finished observing on 15 January 2025 and was switched off on 27 March 2025. The next big catalogue, with data from the first five and a half years, comes out on 2 December 2026.
strumenti/gaia/scoperte: It discovered that the Milky Way "swallowed" a smaller galaxy billions of years ago (Gaia-Enceladus). In 2024 it found Gaia BH3, a dormant black hole of 33 solar masses less than 2,000 light years away: the largest black hole of stellar origin known in our galaxy.
strumenti/gaia/origine: It was meant to be an acronym (Global Astrometric Interferometer for Astrophysics). The project later changed, but the name of the Greek goddess of the Earth stuck.
strumenti/gaia/curiosita: Its measurements are so fine that from Gaia you could see a coin on the Moon. Some of the data were processed in Turin.
strumenti/hipparcos/cosa: The first satellite built to measure the positions and distances of stars. It belonged to ESA and is Gaia's "grandfather".
strumenti/hipparcos/dove: It was supposed to sit in a fixed orbit above the Earth, but the engine that was meant to take it up there didn't fire. It worked all the same, on an elongated orbit.
strumenti/hipparcos/quando: Launched on 8 August 1989, it worked until 1993. The catalogue came out in 1997.
strumenti/hipparcos/scoperte: Precise distances for 118,000 stars, and positions for more than a million others: for twenty years the foundation of all stellar astronomy.
strumenti/hipparcos/origine: A double meaning: it stands for High Precision Parallax Collecting Satellite, and it is the name of Hipparchus of Nicaea, the Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BC who made the first great star catalogue.
strumenti/hipparcos/curiosita: Hipparchus also invented "magnitudes", the brightness scale for stars that is still used today, from the first (the brightest) to the sixth magnitude.
strumenti/cobe/nome: COBE, the light of the Big Bang
strumenti/cobe/cosa: A NASA satellite built to study the cosmic microwave background: the oldest light in the universe, given off 380,000 years after the Big Bang and now a faint glow of microwaves.
strumenti/cobe/dove: In orbit around the Earth, at about 900 km.
strumenti/cobe/scoperte: It measured that this light has exactly the spectrum predicted by the Big Bang theory and, in 1992, found the tiny temperature differences from which the galaxies grew. Nobel Prize 2006 for John Mather and George Smoot.
strumenti/cobe/curiosita: Stephen Hawking called the COBE maps "the discovery of the century, if not of all time".
strumenti/planck/cosa: An ESA satellite that made the most accurate map of the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe, following on from COBE and the American probe WMAP.
strumenti/planck/dove: At the L2 point, 1.5 million km from the Earth.
strumenti/planck/quando: Launched on 14 May 2009 together with the Herschel infrared telescope; switched off in October 2013.
strumenti/planck/scoperte: It measured the age of the universe (13.8 billion years) and its recipe: only 5% is ordinary matter, about 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy.
strumenti/planck/origine: Named after Max Planck, the German physicist and father of quantum theory, Nobel Prize 1918.
strumenti/planck/curiosita: One of its two instruments, LFI, was led by Italy. The other was cooled to a tenth of a degree above absolute zero: for a while it was the coldest known object in space.
strumenti/euclid/cosa: An ESA telescope with a 1.2-metre mirror and a very wide field of view, which over six years will photograph a third of the sky and billions of galaxies to find out what dark matter and dark energy are.
strumenti/euclid/dove: At the L2 point, 1.5 million km from the Earth.
strumenti/euclid/quando: Launched on 1 July 2023. First images in November 2023, first public data in 2025.
strumenti/euclid/scoperte: In 2025 it published its first maps with 26 million galaxies and found an almost perfect "Einstein ring" around a nearby galaxy (NGC 6505), an effect predicted by relativity.
strumenti/euclid/origine: Named after Euclid of Alexandria, the Greek mathematician and father of geometry: the mission measures the "geometry" of the universe.
strumenti/euclid/curiosita: Italy, through ASI and INAF, is one of the countries that contributed most to its instruments and data analysis.
strumenti/soho/cosa: An ESA and NASA observatory that watches the Sun non-stop: it studies its interior, its corona and the solar wind, and warns of solar storms heading towards the Earth.
strumenti/soho/dove: 1.5 million km from the Earth, towards the Sun, at the L1 balance point.
strumenti/soho/quando: Launched on 2 December 1995: it was meant to last two years, and it has been working for thirty.
strumenti/soho/scoperte: It has discovered more comets than anything else in history: more than 5,000, almost all small comets that skim past the Sun. Most of them were found by enthusiasts all over the world looking at its images on the Internet.
strumenti/soho/origine: Short for Solar and Heliospheric Observatory.
strumenti/soho/curiosita: In 1998 mission control lost contact with it for three months and gave it up for lost: they managed to recover it with the big Arecibo radio telescope, which found it again in space.
strumenti/solar-orbiter/cosa: An ESA probe, built with NASA, that goes closer to the Sun than Mercury and, by gradually tilting its orbit, can look at the Sun's poles, which have never been seen before.
strumenti/solar-orbiter/dove: On an orbit around the Sun that brings it to about 42 million km from it on each pass.
strumenti/solar-orbiter/scoperte: In 2020 it saw thousands of tiny flares, nicknamed "campfires". In 2025 it sent back the first images of the Sun's south pole.
strumenti/solar-orbiter/origine: An "orbiter" is a probe that goes round a celestial body: "the one that goes round the Sun".
strumenti/solar-orbiter/curiosita: On board is Metis, a coronagraph built in Italy that "switches off" the disc of the Sun so it can photograph the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere.
strumenti/parker/luce: Direct measurements of the solar wind, fields and particles
strumenti/parker/cosa: A NASA probe that "touches" the Sun: it flies through the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, protected by an 11 cm thick carbon shield that reaches about 1,400 degrees.
strumenti/parker/dove: On a very elongated orbit around the Sun, which brings it within 6.1 million km of its surface.
strumenti/parker/quando: Launched on 12 August 2018. Its closest pass to the Sun was on 24 December 2024.
strumenti/parker/scoperte: It discovered that the solar wind is full of sudden "U-turns" in the magnetic field (switchbacks) and measured close up where they come from.
strumenti/parker/origine: Named after Eugene Parker, the physicist who predicted the solar wind in 1958. It is the first NASA mission named after a living person: Parker, aged 91, watched the launch.
strumenti/parker/curiosita: It is the fastest object ever built: near the Sun it travels at about 690,000 km/h, fast enough to get from Rome to Milan in under three seconds.
strumenti/voyager/luce: Cameras and instruments for particles and fields
strumenti/voyager/cosa: Two twin NASA probes that visited the giant planets and are now travelling through the space between the stars. Voyager 1 is the human-made object furthest from the Earth.
strumenti/voyager/dove: Beyond the reach of the solar wind: Voyager 1 more than 25 billion km away, Voyager 2 more than 20 billion.
strumenti/voyager/quando: Launched in 1977 (Voyager 2 on 20 August, Voyager 1 on 5 September). Voyager 1 left the heliosphere, the Sun's "bubble", in 2012; Voyager 2 in 2018.
strumenti/voyager/scoperte: Active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io (1979), new rings and moons of Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 is still the only probe ever to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).
strumenti/voyager/curiosita: Both carry a golden record with sounds and pictures of the Earth, meant for any extraterrestrials who might find it. On 14 February 1990 Voyager 1 turned round and photographed the Earth from 6 billion km away: the "Pale Blue Dot". Towards the end of 2026 Voyager 1 will be one light-day from us: its signals will take 24 hours to arrive.
strumenti/cassini/cosa: A large probe from NASA, ESA and the Italian Space Agency that studied Saturn, its rings and its moons for 13 years. It carried the European probe Huygens, which landed on Titan.
strumenti/cassini/dove: In orbit around Saturn from 2004 to 2017.
strumenti/cassini/quando: Launched on 15 October 1997. Huygens landed on Titan on 14 January 2005: the most distant landing ever made. On 15 September 2017 Cassini deliberately plunged into Saturn.
strumenti/cassini/scoperte: Jets of water shooting out of the south pole of the moon Enceladus, from an ocean hidden beneath the ice. Lakes and seas of liquid methane on Titan. New moons and details of the rings.
strumenti/cassini/origine: Named after Giovanni Domenico Cassini, an astronomer from Liguria born in Perinaldo in 1625, who discovered four moons of Saturn and the "Cassini Division" in the rings; and after Christiaan Huygens, the Dutchman who discovered Titan in 1655.
strumenti/cassini/curiosita: Cassini's large dish antenna and part of its radar were Italian. The final plunge was to avoid any risk of contaminating, with bacteria from Earth, the moons where there might be life.
strumenti/new-horizons/cosa: The NASA probe that showed us Pluto close up for the first time, the dwarf planet at the edge of the Solar System.
strumenti/new-horizons/dove: In the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune, more than 60 times the distance between the Earth and the Sun.
strumenti/new-horizons/quando: Launched on 19 January 2006. It flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015 and past Arrokoth on 1 January 2019.
strumenti/new-horizons/scoperte: On Pluto, a large heart-shaped plain of ice, mountains of water ice and a thin blue atmosphere. Arrokoth, shaped like a snowman, is the most distant object ever visited by a probe.
strumenti/new-horizons/origine: The name speaks for itself: new horizons to explore.
strumenti/new-horizons/curiosita: On board are the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the American who discovered Pluto in 1930.
strumenti/rosetta/cosa: An ESA probe that travelled alongside a comet for two years on its journey around the Sun, and the Philae lander, the first object to touch down on a comet.
strumenti/rosetta/dove: Around comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, discovered in 1969 by two Soviet astronomers.
strumenti/rosetta/quando: Launched on 2 March 2004, it reached the comet in August 2014. Philae touched down on 12 November 2014. Rosetta ended its mission by descending onto the comet on 30 September 2016.
strumenti/rosetta/scoperte: The comet is shaped like a rubber duck. Rosetta found organic molecules on it and an amino acid, glycine, one of the building blocks of life; the comet's water, however, is different from the water in our oceans.
strumenti/rosetta/origine: From the Rosetta Stone, which made it possible to decipher hieroglyphs: the probe was meant to help "decipher" the origins of the Solar System. Philae is the island in the Nile where an obelisk was found that completed the decipherment.
strumenti/rosetta/curiosita: Philae bounced twice and ended up in shadow, with no sunlight for its batteries. It was only spotted in photos in September 2016, wedged in a crevice. The drill that was meant to bore into the ground was Italian.
